video_title: Mike Milken: Who Gets Access to Capital? | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Mike Milken explains how Depression-era data showed sub-investment-grade debt was overcompensated for risk while sovereigns were the worst credit, how high yield financed MCI, cable, casinos and biotech, and why private credit is essentially public junk debt with 3-5x fees whose real risk is maturity mismatch (SVB, Schwab). He also flags the UAE overtaking the US as top millionaire destination, intra-US migration to Texas/Florida, and health care as the source of over half of global growth.

insights.claim: Milken's study of Depression-era credit research showed that lower-quality debt delivered the highest risk-adjusted returns in the 1930s because risk premiums on sub-investment-grade bonds were too large.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Structural overcompensation for default risk in junk debt is the historical basis for owning high yield through cycles.
insights.quote: the highest rate of return was the lower quality of the debt you bought. In other words, the risk premiums were too large.

insights.claim: Sovereign debt, then treated as riskless and rated AAA, was historically the worst credit; Venezuela was rated AAA while it had 30% unemployment.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Ratings and regulatory 'riskless' treatment of sovereigns can diverge sharply from fundamentals; don't outsource sovereign credit analysis to ratings.
insights.quote: It also showed that the worst credit in history was sovereign debt.

insights.claim: 99.99% of companies in the world are not investment grade, so a market restricted to investment-grade issuers excludes almost all businesses.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: The addressable market for sub-IG lending (public HY and private credit) is structurally vast.
insights.quote: 99.99% of every company in the world is not investment grade.

insights.claim: In the early 1970s Milken showed his own firm that the debt of companies whose stock it recommended buying was sub-investment-grade while the debt of companies it recommended selling was investment grade, arguing that if you like the equity you should like the senior debt.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Cross-check equity conviction against the capital structure: senior debt of a favoured equity can offer better risk-adjusted exposure.
insights.quote: I quietly reminded them that the debt is senior to the equity.

insights.claim: 1974 was the most important financial-market period since the Depression: stocks fell 50%, rates doubled and banks faced credit controls, and buyers of straight non-investment-grade debt made 100% from end-1974 through 1976.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Crisis-era junk spreads have historically produced outsized recoveries; dislocations are when to buy high yield.
insights.quote: you made 100% on your money buying straight non-investment grade debt by the end of 74 through 76.

insights.claim: In the 1950s-60s insurance companies held most high-yield bonds and carried them at internal ratings well above market ratings, and they lobbied Milken not to issue public debt that would expose BB/B ratings on bonds they booked as BBB or A.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Private marks held by long-duration institutions can sit far above market-implied ratings — a parallel worth watching in today's private credit.

insights.claim: Early high-yield issuance in the 1970s financed energy, early biotech, cable, homebuilders, hospitality and the casino industry, which Milken's own firm initially refused to fund; by the late 1980s casino company Mirage was the second most admired company in America.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Sectors shunned by incumbent lenders can become mainstream winners; capital access precedes industry formation.

insights.claim: AT&T, the largest AAA-rated company and largest payer of fees, pressured banks not to finance challengers like MCI; MCI's financing helped cut long-distance call costs (then $10 a minute) by 75%.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Incumbent fee-payers can suppress financing for disruptors; lenders willing to break that pressure capture the disruption upside.
insights.quote: MCI's success and financing them reduced that by 75%.

insights.claim: More than 60 million US jobs were created in the last 30 years of the 20th century by non-investment-grade companies versus minus 4 million by investment-grade companies.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Growth and employment creation comes from sub-IG issuers, supporting the long-run case for growth-oriented credit.
insights.quote: more than 60 million jobs were created in the last 30 years of the 20th century by non-investment grade companies and minus4 million jobs were created by investment grade companies.

insights.claim: Milken's prosperity formula: access to capital and financial technology act as a multiplier on human capital (the largest asset), social capital and real assets; transformative ideas like mobile and AI need significant investment and belief in the future.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Frames capital markets' role in funding AI-scale buildouts — the financing channel matters as much as the idea.

insights.claim: Milken prioritised the people and their vision over balance sheets when backing founders such as Malone, Turner and Murdoch, and says he would not have funded any CEO who told him they were in it for the money.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Founder motivation and vision are core underwriting inputs, especially in growth credit and venture-like lending.
insights.quote: I think people were infatuated by balance sheets.

insights.claim: Citing Gary Becker's human-capital work, Milken estimates US human and social capital at more than $2,000 trillion versus about $300 trillion in financial assets and roughly $30 trillion GDP.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Policies that erode human/social capital (talent flows, education) can matter more to long-run returns than financial balance sheets.

insights.claim: New industries are always considered risky while investors underestimate the risks in incumbent industries of the past.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Systematically lean toward mispriced new-industry credit and be skeptical of 'safe' legacy incumbents.
insights.quote: new industries are always considered to be risky and industries of the past people underestimate the risk.

insights.claim: Securitization was one of Milken's six 1960s goals: pooling car loans, mortgages and credit cards spreads risk geographically and across borrowers, lowering consumer borrowing rates and reducing lending bias.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Diversified pooling underpins cheaper consumer credit and now extends to royalties, music rights and sports teams.

insights.claim: Traditional TV and cable are highly dependent on sports and marquee live events; if those move off traditional television, viewership will plummet and the survival of legacy media is in question — YouTube will broadcast the Academy Awards from 2029.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Live-rights migration to streaming is a key risk to legacy media equity and debt and a tailwind for YouTube/Alphabet.
insights.quote: beginning in 2029, YouTube will be broadcasting the Academy Awards.

insights.claim: Private credit is essentially no different from public non-investment-grade debt — a throwback to the 1950s-60s when insurers were the largest lenders — except managers charge roughly three to five times higher fees.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Question the fee premium for private credit versus public HY with similar credit risk.
insights.quote: private credit to me is really no different than public credit for the money manager. They get to charge you more money

insights.claim: Private credit's strength is that 95-99% of investors are long-term holders; quarterly individual redemptions at major managers are a very small share of assets (perhaps 1%), so the key is keeping capital with long-term investors like pension funds and insurers.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Redemption headlines at retail-facing private credit vehicles may be less systemic than feared; watch the share of short-term capital.

insights.claim: The major losses in the 2007-10 financial crisis were in securities perceived as investment grade — particularly real-estate-backed paper rated AAA, AA or A — not in non-investment-grade debt.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Ratings-driven complacency, not junk exposure, causes the biggest blowups; scrutinise highly rated structured credit.

insights.claim: Mismatch of asset and liability maturities is one of the greatest financial-market risks: Silicon Valley Bank and Republic failed not from credit losses but from funding US government securities with short-term liabilities as rates rose, and Schwab's stock fell 40% for similar reasons.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Screen lenders and credit holders for duration mismatch first; rate volatility, not defaults, is the near-term failure mode.
insights.quote: one of the greatest risk in financial markets is mismatch of maturities and investments.

insights.claim: Milken's first check on financial markets is whether the holders of assets have capital locked at fixed rates for long periods; the second is tracking major movements of assets and people.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: A two-step risk checklist: liability structure of holders, then capital/talent flows.

insights.claim: Apollo has recently been a leader in lending to SoftBank for its AI investments, illustrating that lender decisions matter for new ventures, whereas lending to Microsoft makes no difference because tens of thousands of lenders compete for it.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Alpha in credit lies in financing new ideas where capital is scarce, not crowded megacap lending; AI capex is increasingly credit-funded.
insights.quote: Apollo has been a leader recently in loaning money to SoftBank for their AI investments today.

insights.claim: In 2023 or 2024 the UAE overtook the US as the number one destination for millionaires, with the US second and Singapore third, ending more than a century of US dominance in attracting human capital.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Flows of entrepreneurs and wealth signal where future companies and jobs will be created.
insights.quote: the number one destination for millionaires in the world was the UAE. US was second, Singapore was third.

insights.claim: Entrepreneurs and wealthy individuals moving from Northern Europe and the UK to Greece, Italy or the UAE raises the question of whether future companies will be born in their origin countries.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Tax-driven migration could erode Europe's new-company formation; favour destinations attracting founders.

insights.claim: Within the US, people and companies are leaving California for Texas, Florida, Nevada and Tennessee; Palantir moved its headquarters to Florida and Elon Musk's departure may cost California $100 billion over time while SpaceX creates millionaire employees in Texas.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: State-level talent migration shifts tax bases and job creation; relevant for muni credit and regional growth.

insights.claim: Milken believes the US could once have paid off its debt using its social capital, e.g. by selling green cards to wealthy foreigners, but damaging its appeal to entrepreneurs risks the best and brightest staying elsewhere; nearly all of the 20 most valuable companies are American.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Erosion of US attractiveness to global talent is a long-run risk to US exceptionalism and its fiscal position.

insights.claim: Milken argues more than 50% of all economic growth in the world has come from advances in health care and public health.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Health-care innovation is a primary macro growth driver, supporting long-term allocation to bioscience.
insights.quote: more than 50% of all economic growth in the world has come from advances in health care and public health

insights.claim: Global life expectancy rose from 31 in 1900 to the mid-70s today, an extension of more than 40 years in 120 years versus 11 years over 4 million years of evolution.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Longevity gains are a durable economic force; longevity-related sectors benefit.

insights.claim: Milken expects heart disease and cancer, the major causes of death in the Western world, to be substantially reduced within the next decade or two through new developments; he invests both philanthropically and in for-profit health businesses.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Oncology and cardiology innovation is a long-duration investment theme; Novo Nordisk was briefly Europe's most valuable company before tech overtook it.

insights.claim: In the 1970s about one in four finance recruits said they joined to change the world; today maybe 1% do, which Milken attributes to soaring valuations and compensation at financial institutions and money managers.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: A finance industry driven by pay rather than mission may underinvest in financing new ideas and weaken public trust.

insights.claim: Financial institutions have failed to explain their role in society; with rising prices and affordability problems, most people now question the financial system, as seen in backlash against Goldman's 'God's work' remark and Amgen's 1994 fall from most-admired industry.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Political and regulatory risk for finance and pharma rises when public trust erodes over affordability.

insights.claim: Milken learned that facts alone don't persuade — a financial-institution head once said he'd buy junk debt only if the Knicks won — so he shifted to asking questions and letting investors reach conclusions through self-discovery.
insights.speaker: Mike Milken
insights.so_what: Investor behaviour is often non-fundamental; persuasion works better through guided self-discovery than data dumps.
insights.quote: If the Knicks win, I'll buy it. And if the Knicks lose, I won't.
